summary: Nine labels print horse chestnut seed extract at 250 to 500 mg with no aescin in the rows, and two carry a metabolic claim, not a venous one. This is the strongest evidence in this batch: Cochrane's 2012 update of oral mono-preparations reports less leg pain in six of seven placebo-controlled trials and a 32.1 mL leg volume difference, short term, with caveats (23152216). A 240-patient trial of 50 mg aescin twice daily reduced leg volume versus placebo and was equivalent to compression stockings (8569363), though its abstract says efficacy (oedema reduction) rather than primary outcome. Against this, extract was not superior to placebo in advanced disease (11747472) and ulcer healing was not significantly different in an underpowered trial (16620045). The studied doses are stated as aescin, while the labels print extract mass, except one comparison at 600 mg/d (8737631). Abstracts, plus full text passages for 11747472.
question_for_clinician: Does Cochrane 23152216 and the 240-patient trial 8569363 (50 mg aescin twice daily) support credit for seed extract labels that print 250 to 500 mg of extract with no aescin in the rows and no venous claim? Agent recommendation: no credit for these rows, because the studied aescin dose can't be matched to them. The evidence itself is not weak, so a label printing aescin at the studied dose would be a different question.
